title: Paul's grief (Romans 9–10)
hook: Paul aches for his own Jewish people; how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news

segments.voice: Yesterday, the peak of Romans: neither death nor life, nor height nor depth. Your line was nothing can separate us. When a fear showed up, did you answer it? Day three hundred twenty-four.

You've just had the best news of your life, and you run home to share it, and the people you love most, your own family, see it differently. You don't stop loving them. It aches. Paul has just written the most soaring lines in the letter: nothing can separate us from the love of God. And the very next sentence, the mood drops like a stone. He's not thinking about Rome anymore. He's thinking about his own family, his own people, the Jewish people. Chapters nine through eleven are Paul wrestling, out loud, with grief and hope at the same time.
screen: `THE BEST NEWS, AND YOUR FAMILY.` → `THE MOOD DROPS LIKE A STONE.` → `GRIEF AND HOPE AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Paul writes, in the King James Bible: "That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart." Continual. Not a passing sadness. He says he'd almost give up his own place with Christ if it would help his kinsmen. Then he lists what belongs to his people, and it's a list of honors: "Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises." The patriarchs are theirs, and Jesus himself, Paul says, came from them. Paul never stops being a Jew, and he speaks of his people with love. His grief is that most of them haven't received Jesus as Messiah, and chapters nine and ten turn that over and over, painfully, without easy answers. Then in chapter ten he widens the door: there is no difference, he says, between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is rich to all who call on him. And he asks: how will anyone hear unless someone is sent? And he quotes the prophet Isaiah: "How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!" Feet. Not faces, not voices. Dusty feet that walked the long road to bring the news. Now something honest. For centuries, some Christians used these chapters to look down on Jewish people, and that contempt fed real cruelty. Since the Holocaust, many churches, Catholic and Protestant, have firmly rejected it and affirmed God's lasting love for the Jewish people. Churches still differ on how to understand Paul's hope today. But they read him now as he wrote: aching with love, not contempt.
screen: `GREAT HEAVINESS AND CONTINUAL SORROW.` · `THE ADOPTION, THE COVENANTS, THE PROMISES.` · `NO DIFFERENCE: THE SAME LORD OVER ALL.` · `DUSTY FEET THAT BRING GOOD NEWS.` · then, large: `HOW BEAUTIFUL ARE THE FEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for the Jewish people. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind Jewish people you know, or a synagogue near you, or Jewish communities around the world, many of which face real hatred today. Hold them in mind with the love Paul had for his own family. If you pray, you can pray for their peace, their safety and their joy. If you don't, simply wish them well with each breath out. Then think of someone whose feet brought good news to you once, and give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Paul's grief. His continual sorrow for his own people, spoken with love, and the beautiful feet of those who carry good news.
Your line: beautiful feet. Today, carry one piece of good news to someone on purpose: a thank-you, a compliment, some news that will lift them. Walk it over if you can. Day three hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Many churches today pray for the Jewish people in their regular intercessions, and Catholics pray for them by name in the Good Friday liturgy; Christians read Romans 9–11 with care since the Holocaust.

original.note: Greek: beautiful. from hōra, hour or season: lovely because it comes at just the right time.

trapdoor: what you thought: beautiful feet is a strange compliment.
what it means: Paul, grieving for his own people, quotes Isaiah on the messengers whose dusty feet carry good news of peace.
what a scholar hears: hōraioi is related to hōra, the hour or season, so the feet may be lovely because they come at the right time; Paul is quoting a Greek form of Isaiah 52:7.

notes: SENSITIVE DAY. The outline practice 'pray for the Jewish people' is framed as prayer for their peace, safety and joy, not for conversion. Keeper (and ideally a Jewish reader) should review. Romans 10:1 ('that they might be saved') is cited but not quoted; the script says Paul's grief is that most of his people had not received Jesus as Messiah. Confirm this is honest to the text and not hurtful.

'Since the Holocaust, many churches, Catholic and Protestant, have firmly rejected' contempt: Nostra Aetate (1965) and many Protestant statements. Confirm wording; 'churches still differ on how to understand Paul's hope today' covers the range from dual-covenant views to continued evangelism.
howItsDone: the Catholic Good Friday solemn intercessions include a prayer for the Jewish people; confirm.

Hōraios / hōra etymology and the 'right time' sense: confirm. Paul's quotation of Isaiah 52:7 is closer to the Hebrew than the Septuagint in places; the trapdoor says 'a Greek form of Isaiah 52:7', which is deliberately loose.
